part_title: DNS Fundamentals, Resolver Roles and Split-Horizon Views

scenes.title: DNS answers a name; routing carries the traffic
scenes.visual_overview: Two panels separate DNS resolving app.internal to 10.20.1.25 from the subsequent TLS connection to that address.
visual_walkthrough: Follow the client query and Resolver answer
Trace the TCP 443 request through routes, security group and NACL
Explain TTL and the difference between DNS success and application reachability
scenes.visual_example: The resolver can return a private IP even when a security group blocks port 443.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Troubleshoot DNS, address, route and application as distinct steps.
scenes.narration: The slide is divided into two steps that must not be confused. Start on the left. A client queries the VPC Resolver for app dot internal. The resolver returns ten dot twenty dot one dot twenty five. That answer tells the client where the service might be reached; it does not establish a connection. Now move to the right. The client initiates TLS to that address on port four four three. Its packets must follow a valid VPC route, pass applicable security group permissions and comply with network ACL rules, including the return path. Look at the bottom warnings. A successful DNS answer can coexist with a failed application connection. The resolver does not proxy the application flow, and cached answers follow their TTL, so changes are not necessarily immediate. In a troubleshooting scenario, inspect the returned name and address first. Next validate source and destination route tables, effective security rules, TCP connectivity and finally application health. Never treat a valid DNS response as proof that an endpoint is reachable.

scenes.title: Who knows the answer? DNS roles and caching
scenes.visual_overview: Client, recursive resolver cache and authoritative DNS are arranged in three columns with a numbered query and response sequence.
visual_walkthrough: Start at the client stub resolver
Examine positive cache and TTL at recursive resolver
Explain authoritative record source and negative caching
Follow the response arrow and implications of record changes
scenes.visual_example: A cached A record with 300-second TTL can outlive an authoritative DNS edit until its cache expires.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Identify the answering resolver and its cache before changing the zone again.
scenes.narration: Begin on the left with the client stub resolver, whose job is to request DNS information. The client sends its question to the recursive resolver in the central panel. This resolver may already have a record cached, like the example A record with a three hundred second time to live. In that case it answers directly while the cached data remains valid. If the answer is not cached, the recursive process obtains information from the appropriate authoritative servers. The authoritative zone shown on the right contains record types such as A, AAAA, MX and TXT. Follow the numbered arrows back from the zone to the recursive resolver and then to the client. At the bottom, the positive cache box describes normal records. The negative cache box describes responses such as NXDOMAIN or the absence of a requested record type; negative answers can also be cached. The orange warning explains why changing a record does not flush resolver caches. For SAP-level operations, find which resolver the client actually used and whether a TTL or negative cached response explains the discrepancy.

scenes.title: Split-horizon DNS: same name, different view
scenes.visual_overview: An internet query reaches the public zone and public ALB, while an associated VPC query uses the private zone and private ALB.
visual_walkthrough: Trace the public DNS answer for app.example.com
Compare the VPC Resolver and associated private zone answer
Explain delegation, VPC DNS settings and private-zone association
Explain why a private-zone miss does not fall back automatically to the public zone
scenes.visual_example: Internal employees can receive a private ALB answer while external customers receive a public ALB answer for the same hostname.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The caller's DNS view and networking reachability both matter.
scenes.narration: This slide shows how two clients can resolve exactly the same name but receive different targets. The orange diagram on the left represents a client on the internet querying public DNS for app dot example dot com. The public hosted zone has a record pointing toward an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. Now compare the cyan diagram on the right. A client in an associated VPC asks the Amazon VPC Resolver, which consults the private hosted zone for the matching name. That zone can point the same hostname to an internal load balancer. Read the three numbered cards below. The public domain must be delegated correctly for public resolution. A private hosted zone must be associated with the relevant VPC, which also needs appropriate DNS settings. If that private zone matches a domain but does not contain the requested name or record type, the resolver does not automatically fetch the public record as a fallback. In troubleshooting, first identify the client's resolver and zone visibility. Remember that getting a private address and actually reaching it are separate design questions.
